Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 11:15 AM PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Tom Hargreaves (Aurelius CTO), Leah Kim (Aurelius Cloud Eng), Amir Sadiq (Aurelius Security)
Recording: yes
Notes: deep dive focused on Private VPC networking and runtime performance (KV cache, batching, quant, latency SLOs)
summary: Deep technical session walking through Aurelius's Private VPC architecture and Redwood runtime networking requirements. Discussed PrivateLink vs VPC peering, NAT behaviour for autoscaling nodes, subnet sizing, DNS and route tables, TLS termination and KMS, performance implications for KV cache and batching, and next steps for a pilot benchmark.
topics: NAT gateways and egress behaviour for private instances
KV cache & batching impact on throughput
TLS termination and KMS/HSM for private deployments
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the private VPC networking details and runtime implications — should be about 50 minutes, we'll take notes and action items
[00:08] Tom Hargreaves: great, thanks Maya. we've got Leah and Amir here; main goals — we want predictable p95 latency under 200ms for inference, and keep data inside our VPC. also curious about how KV cache and batching will affect network patterns
[00:22] Carlos Ruiz: perfect, quick intro from our side — I'm Carlos, I own runtime networking and perf. i'll walk through networking patterns, interface endpoints (PrivateLink), NAT, and how the runtime interacts with the cache. expect rough numbers, we'll validate in the pilot
[00:35] Leah Kim: quick note — we're on AWS, EKS-backed, currently have private subnets with NAT gateway egress and strict NACLs. we also use internal DNS and have cross-account peering for some infra
[00:46] Carlos Ruiz: ok, common pattern. first key question: do you want Redwood's runtime inside your VPC with interface endpoints to our control plane, or fully customer-managed runtime that we install on your ASG? there's tradeoffs on maintenance and network surfaces
[00:58] Tom Hargreaves: prefer Redwood-managed but inside our VPC — we want minimal ops. is PrivateLink the common approach? how does that affect latency
[01:10] Carlos Ruiz: yes, PrivateLink (AWS interface endpoints) is our recommended pattern for control plane comms — it keeps traffic on AWS network and avoids public internet. Data plane (inference) can run in your VPC, and uses ENIs to talk to model servers. latency impact for control calls is small — tens of ms — main latency is model inference itself
[01:24] Amir Sadiq: on egress and compliance — we need to ensure KMS calls and metrics don't traverse public internet, and we want audit logs in our S3 bucket with SSE-KMS
[01:35] Maya Patel: we support VPC endpoints for metrics, KMS is customer-managed and our control plane can integrate via PrivateLink to avoid public egress. we'll share our runbook with the exact endpoint service name
[01:46] Carlos Ruiz: network details — runtime workers in your private subnets will need appropriate route tables and security group rules. ENIs per instance are limited by instance type; for large inference instances we typically recommend /24 or /23 sized subnets per AZ depending on scale
[02:05] Leah Kim: can you expand on ENI limits and pod density? we use EKS so pods get IPs from worker nodes
[02:14] Carlos Ruiz: yeah — ENI limits mean on some instances you may hit IP exhaustion if pods are dense. we recommend using CNI modifications (e.g., AWS VPC CNI with prefix delegation) or use Bottlerocket/container-optimized AMIs with ip-masq disabled for better throughput. for very high throughput, dedicated nodes per model pool helps
[02:36] Tom Hargreaves: and about NAT — when the runtime spins up new nodes or autoscaling, do calls to our internal control plane or KMS go through NAT? we want to avoid hairpinning
[02:47] Carlos Ruiz: Good point. If the control plane is accessible via PrivateLink, no NAT required for control plane traffic. Egress for pulling container images or external package access will go through NAT — recommend using ECR VPC endpoints and S3 endpoints to reduce NAT usage. NAT Gateway can add tens to low hundreds of ms during cold starts depending on concurrent connections
[03:10] Maya Patel: also note TCP connection ramp-up — when many pods start, you can get SYN floods to KMS or control plane if not using endpoints which increases p95 briefly. the pilot will measure warmup
[03:22] Leah Kim: DNS — we have private hosted zones and conditional forwarding. how does Redwood expect DNS to be configured for instance discovery and for PrivateLink
[03:32] Carlos Ruiz: we prefer customers create interface endpoints and set up route53 private hosted zones with CNAMEs pointing to the endpoint DNS names. our runbook has exact records. If you use custom DNS resolvers, ensure they forward AWS private zone queries — otherwise resolve timeouts can add 50–100ms
[03:53] Amir Sadiq: any special TLS considerations? we terminate TLS at runtime but also need to ensure keys never leave our KMS
[03:59] Carlos Ruiz: by default, our runtime will terminate TLS inside your VPC and you can configure mutual TLS for control-plane calls. For model encryption at rest and key wrapping we integrate with customer KMS; private deployments can leverage HSM-backed KMS for FIPS requirements
[04:14] Tom Hargreaves: how does KV cache work across nodes? is it local to a node or shared via a cache tier that would add network hops
[04:22] Carlos Ruiz: our KV cache is primarily local per model shard to avoid network hops on the critical path. we do support a distributed cache tier (Redis/ElastiCache) for large prefix reuse but that adds network latency; typical pattern is local KV per pod + optional warm-up from central store. local cache means most inference calls avoid cross-node RPCs
[04:41] Leah Kim: what's the network pattern for batching — do workers send larger payloads upstream or is batching local to the GPU?
[04:48] Carlos Ruiz: batching is handled in-process at the runtime layer — we aggregate requests for the same model shard and send a single CUDA kernel invocation. From a networking perspective batching reduces number of requests to the model server but increases per-request payload sizes slightly due to concatenated contexts. If you are CPU-bound pre/post processing will still be per-request though
[05:10] Maya Patel: note that batching impacts p99 tail: large batches help throughput but can increase single-request latency if your SLO is per-request; we can tune batch size and max latency to strike a balance
[05:22] Amir Sadiq: quantization — do smaller model sizes reduce network I/O? does it change KV cache behavior
[05:28] Carlos Ruiz: quantization reduces model memory footprint and may change cache hit behavior (smaller KV entries), so slightly reduces IO for model transfer at startup. But per-token network I/O is dominated by control and telemetry rather than model payloads; quantization mainly helps CPU/GPU latency and memory usage
[05:45] Tom Hargreaves: autoscaling: when we scale from zero to X nodes, any network hotspots we should watch for
[05:52] Carlos Ruiz: yes ramping causes connection churn to control plane and to any central stores; to minimize, we recommend warm pools for model shards and pre-warming KV caches. We also have adaptive retries in the runtime for short connection errors
[06:05] Leah Kim: what about packet MTU and fragmentation — we have jumbo frames enabled internally, any issues?
[06:10] Carlos Ruiz: jumbo frames are fine but ensure consistent MTU across path. Fragmentation can hurt cold-start transfers of large model artifacts, best to use S3 endpoints and segmented downloads with parallelism. For PrivateLink the MTU is typically 1500; document checks in our runbook
[06:30] Tom Hargreaves: can you support cross-account endpoints? we host infra across multiple accounts
[06:36] Carlos Ruiz: yes PrivateLink supports cross-account; you just need to accept the endpoint service in the account hosting the endpoints and we provide the service name. We'll include template CloudFormation for the endpoint creation
[06:47] Maya Patel: security check — audit logs, SSO and RBAC? we support SAML/SCIM for SSO and we can forward audit events to customer S3 or CloudWatch via PrivateLink
[06:59] Amir Sadiq: good. need retention options, and proof of tamper evidence
[07:05] Carlos Ruiz: we include signed audit logs; retention policies are configurable and we can push logs to your bucket using VPC endpoints and S3 access points
[07:16] Leah Kim: earlier you mentioned metrics — where do they ship? we need in internal Grafana and not to public endpoints
[07:23] Maya Patel: metrics can be forwarded to your internal Prometheus/Grafana through push gateways inside the VPC or to our metrics endpoint over PrivateLink, whichever you prefer; both options require endpoint config
[07:33] Tom Hargreaves: any known perf numbers for p95 end-to-end when using PrivateLink and local runtime for a 4k prompt size
[07:41] Carlos Ruiz: rough numbers: for a 4k prompt on a GPU-optimized shard, inference compute adds ~60–120ms depending on quant model, KV cache hit reduces by ~20–40ms on average; control plane overhead via PrivateLink typically adds 10–30ms. So combined p95 in ideal conditions can be sub-200ms, but depends heavily on kernel, batch sizing, and cold starts
[08:06] Leah Kim: that aligns with our target. curious about burst traffic — will NAT gateways be a bottleneck for egress if we use them for metrics
[08:14] Carlos Ruiz: yes NAT is a common bottleneck; each NAT gateway scales with bandwidth but also SNAT port exhaustion can occur. Avoid NAT for metrics and package pulls by using VPC endpoints for S3/ECR and interface endpoints for metrics/KMS
[08:31] Maya Patel: for the pilot we recommend a dedicated subnet per model pool, interface endpoints for control and KMS, and CloudFormation for quick creation
[08:40] Tom Hargreaves: ok can you share the CFN templates and runbook
[08:45] Carlos Ruiz: yes we'll share templates. Also note one more runtime caveat: UDP-based health checks are not used, we rely on TCP/TLS probes — so security groups must allow those port ranges between nodes
[08:58] Leah Kim: what's the recommended idle timeout for connections? LB idle timeouts sometimes kill long-lived streams
[09:05] Carlos Ruiz: we recommend 60-120s for load balancer idle timeouts, and keepalive on the runtime. For streaming responses, we keep the connection open with periodic heartbeats; if you have aggressive timeouts, streaming will break
[09:20] Maya Patel: let's pause — any other gaps we should cover
[09:24] Amir Sadiq: compliance: we need SOC2 scope and pen-test reports; also need details about key rotation
[09:31] Maya Patel: we've got SOC2 Type II and annual pen-tests; key rotation can be managed by customer KMS and Redwood supports rotating wrapping keys. we'll attach the compliance pack
[09:43] Carlos Ruiz: i want to flag network MTU again in the doc; many customers forget to set consistent MTU and large model pulls can time out
[09:52] Tom Hargreaves: great. can we do a two-hour pilot that runs load with KV cache and batching? measure p50/p95/p99, cold and warm start
[09:59] Carlos Ruiz: yes we can; propose next week Tues/Thu morning slots. we'll need subnet CIDRs, security group rules, and sample prompts
[10:12] Leah Kim: i'll provide CIDRs and sample prompts. also will check with infra for endpoint creation privileges
[10:18] Maya Patel: recap of next steps — we'll send runbook, CFN template, and perf checklist; Carlos will run the pilot and provide results
[10:26] Tom Hargreaves: sounds good
[10:28] Maya Patel: action items — Carlos to prepare benchmark scripts, Maya to send runbook. thanks all
[10:34] Carlos Ruiz: continuing on some deeper points we didn't fully unpack — model rollout strategy in private VPCs. when we roll a new model we can do canary shards in a small subset of nodes to avoid wide blast radius; networking wise that means slightly different SGs and labels so traffic splits cleanly
[11:02] Leah Kim: what about cross-AZ latency? our users are global and want low jitter
[11:10] Carlos Ruiz: best to colocate model pools and client-facing gateways in the same AZ. cross-AZ calls add extra network hop; if you need HA use multi-AZ pools but prefer local routing for latency-sensitive requests
[12:00] [--- mid-call deep technical discussion about kernel selection, attention optimization, and model shard placement omitted for brevity ---]
[28:15] Carlos Ruiz: picking up — KV cache warmers: we can precompute common prefixes and populate local KV so warm requests are fast; this is done over internal control messages which are lightweight and use PrivateLink
[30:02] Leah Kim: any recommended telemetry dimensions we should capture during pilot?
[30:10] Carlos Ruiz: p50/p95/p99 for token latency, batch size distribution, KV hit rate, network RTTs, TLS handshake times, cold-start duration, and number of retransmits. we'll provide a dashboard template
[32:44] Amir Sadiq: can Redwood's control plane trigger edge invalidations if we detect bad cache entries?
[32:51] Carlos Ruiz: yes invalidation APIs exist; for private deployments we can call a signed endpoint over PrivateLink to instruct nodes to expire prefixes
[35:00] Maya Patel: backlog note — we should test quantized 4-bit models in the pilot to see memory pressure and tail latency effect
[36:22] Carlos Ruiz: good call. quantized models reduce memory and may decrease kernel latency but sometimes increase variance, so we'll include both int8 and 4-bit runs in the benchmark
[38:40] Leah Kim: about model artifact distribution — large models are pulled at deploy time; what's the recommended distribution strategy to avoid saturating node network
[38:49] Carlos Ruiz: staggered deployments with download concurrency limits, use S3 multipart with parallel ranged downloads and local disk cache. pre-bake AMIs with common model shards is another pattern to avoid heavy network load on scale events
[41:05] Tom Hargreaves: regarding RBAC, can we map Redwood roles to our internal LDAP groups?
[41:12] Maya Patel: yes SAML/SCIM mapping supports group sync; we can map admin/ops/dev roles to your groups and enforce least privilege for model access and audit viewing
[43:00] [--- runtime logs and crash recovery discussion: crash loops, OOM handling, and network partition mitigation ---]
[46:12] Carlos Ruiz: in partition scenarios the runtime goes into degraded mode: it serves from local cache when possible and rejects writes to central telemetry until connectivity is restored. we log events and surface them via the alerting hooks you configure
[48:30] Leah Kim: curious about TLS session reuse and handshake cost; if we do many short-lived requests is handshake cost significant
[48:38] Carlos Ruiz: yes TLS handshake can add ~10-20ms per new connection; we recommend keepalives and connection pooling. for heavy streaming, mutual tls with session resumption drastically reduces handshake overhead
[50:05] Maya Patel: wrapping up, we're going to provision a test environment for the pilot: one small model pool (2 nodes), one medium (4 nodes), interface endpoints for control/KMS/metrics, and CloudFormation templates to create the subnets and SGs
[50:22] Tom Hargreaves: timeline — if we get CIDRs to you by Fri, can you start next Tue for the two-hour pilot
[50:28] Carlos Ruiz: yes tentative slots available. we'll confirm after runbook and CFN are shared
[51:10] Maya Patel: final notes — we'll also include a checklist for network team: list of required security group rules, route table entries, DNS private hosted zone entries, ECR/S3 endpoints, and expected ENI counts per instance type
[52:00] Leah Kim: thank you, this is super helpful.
[52:12] Amir Sadiq: thanks. security will review the runbook and request any pen-test artifacts as needed
[52:25] Maya Patel: i'll follow up with the runbook, CFN, and perf checklist; Carlos will schedule the pilot and send benchmark scripts
[52:36] Tom Hargreaves: thanks everyone
[54:30] (meeting ends)
